t.textos.atrahasis.pasajes.0.texto: "When the gods, instead of man, / did the work, bore the loads, / the load of the gods was too great".
t.textos.atrahasis.pasajes.0.fuente: Translated into Spanish from W. G. Lambert and A. R. Millard, Atra-ḫasīs: The Babylonian Story of the Flood (1969), I, 1–3 (short quotation), and here into English from the Spanish
t.textos.atrahasis.pasajes.0.nota_academ: The first line, inūma ilū awīlum, is famous for its ambiguity: literally "when the gods (were) man", that is, when the gods performed the role that man would later have, labor. There follows a long passage in which the Igigi dig the Tigris and the Euphrates for 3,600 years, go on strike, burn their hoes and baskets, surround Enlil's Ekur at night and say that all of them have declared war. Enlil wants to punish the ringleader, but Enki (Ea) says that their complaint is just and proposes a solution: to create a being that will bear the labor.
t.textos.atrahasis.pasajes.0.lectura_ast: For Sitchin, and later for Alan Alford (Gods of the New Millennium, 1996) and Michael Tellinger, the rebellion of the Igigi is a mutiny of the Anunnaki astronaut-miners who extracted gold in southern Africa (the Abzu). To replace them, Enki would have created Homo sapiens through genetic engineering.

The Igigi dig rivers and canals, the basic work of Mesopotamian irrigation agriculture; the text does not mention mines or gold. The Apsu/Abzu is the underground ocean of fresh water, with its temple at Eridu, not a region of Africa. The myth projects onto the gods the social structure of forced labor (corvée) and justifies human service in the temples. The "ruins" of Mpumalanga that Tellinger attributes to the Anunnaki are Bokoni farmsteads from the 16th–19th centuries AD.
t.textos.atrahasis.pasajes.0.lectura_act: The strike of the Igigi is often presented as the first story of a labor strike: the workers burn their tools and take a stand before the boss's house. Current readings stress that the conflict is not resolved with justice for the workers but by transferring the labor to another group, humans.
Synthesis of socioeconomic readings; see Tikva Frymer-Kensky, "The Atrahasis Epic and Its Significance for Our Understanding of Genesis 1–9", Biblical Archaeologist 40, 1977
t.textos.atrahasis.pasajes.1.texto: Paraphrase. The gods summon the birth goddess, Nintu (also Mami, Belet-ili), "midwife of the gods", and ask her to create man so that he may bear the yoke. She replies that she cannot do it alone: she needs Enki, who has the clay. Enki establishes a purification rite on the 1st, 7th and 15th days of the month: a god, We-ila, who "had intelligence" (ṭēmu), will be sacrificed, and with his flesh and blood Nintu will mix the clay, so that god and man are mixed together. From the god's flesh a spirit (eṭemmu) remains, so that he may always be remembered. The Igigi spit on the clay. Mami kneads it, recites the incantation, and fourteen womb goddesses form seven males and seven females. After ten months, the goddess opens the womb and humans are born. Birth rites are instituted, such as setting down a brick for the woman in labor for nine days.
t.textos.atrahasis.pasajes.1.fuente: Paraphrase based on Lambert and Millard (1969) and on the revised edition by B. R. Foster, Before the Muses (3rd ed., 2005)
t.textos.atrahasis.pasajes.1.nota_academ: The passage plays on words: ṭēmu ("intelligence, plan") and eṭemmu ("spirit of the dead"), awīlum ("man") and ilu ("god"), so that man carries within himself the reason of the sacrificed god and a soul that survives as a ghost. It is the model for Enuma Elish VI and presents creation as a birth with a midwife, fourteen wombs and ten months of gestation. The Assyrian recensions expand the scene.
t.textos.atrahasis.pasajes.1.lectura_ast: Alan Alford reads the fourteen womb goddesses as surrogate mothers carrying modified embryos, and the mixture of divine blood with clay as the combination of extraterrestrial DNA with that of a hominid (the "clay" would be the earthly genetic material).

The passage follows step by step the practice of childbirth in Mesopotamia (midwife, birth brick, ten lunar months, incantations) and that of the potter working clay. Reading it as genetics requires assuming that the scribes did not understand their own text. The same images of clay and blood appear in the myths of peoples unrelated to one another.
t.textos.atrahasis.pasajes.1.lectura_act: Unlike the Enuma Elish, where a male god creates man, Atrahasis gives the leading role to a mother goddess with midwives and wombs: gender readings stress how the myth sacralizes women's knowledge of childbirth before its displacement by male theologies.
Tikva Frymer-Kensky, In the Wake of the Goddesses, 1992
t.textos.atrahasis.pasajes.2.ref: Assyrian recension, cols. I–II (= Tablet II, iv–vi of the modern edition)
t.textos.atrahasis.pasajes.2.fuente: Spanish version based on R. W. Rogers, Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament (1912), pp. 114–116, translated here into English from the Spanish
t.textos.atrahasis.pasajes.2.nota_academ: Rogers knew only fragments from Ashurbanipal's library and could not place them in the whole; today we know that they belong to the plague of drought and famine in Tablet II, Enlil's third attempt before the flood. His observation that the white fields are salt is correct: the text reflects the salinization of irrigated soils, a real problem in southern Mesopotamia. "Nisaba" is the goddess of grain. The scene of cannibalism is a formula of extreme famine that reappears in the curses of Neo-Assyrian treaties.
t.textos.atrahasis.pasajes.2.lectura_act: The succession of punishments (plague, drought, salinization, famine) is read today as a catalog of the environmental risks of an irrigation civilization: the myth links population growth, soil exhaustion and catastrophe. Anne Draffkorn Kilmer proposed that the central theme of the poem is overpopulation.
Anne D. Kilmer, "The Mesopotamian Concept of Overpopulation and Its Solution as Reflected in the Mythology", Orientalia 41, 1972
t.textos.atrahasis.pasajes.3.texto: Paraphrase. Enki speaks to the wall of Atrahasis's hut: "Wall, listen to me; reed hut, attend to my words". He orders him to pull down the house and build a roofed boat, like the Apsu, with thick bitumen, and to abandon his possessions to save his life. Atrahasis gathers the elders and explains to them that his god Enki is at odds with Enlil and that he can no longer live in their city. He takes his family and the animals on board, but he cannot sit down or eat: his heart is broken. Adad roars in the clouds, the winds break loose, the flood advances like an army and people cannot see one another. For seven days and seven nights the rain falls. Nintu weeps for mankind, who fill the river like dragonflies; the thirsty gods huddle like sheep. When Atrahasis makes a sacrifice, the gods gather like flies. Enlil is enraged when he sees the boat; Enki takes responsibility. It is agreed to limit mankind: there will be women who give birth and women who do not, the demon Pashittu will snatch the child from its mother's lap, and certain priestesses will be taboo for childbearing.
t.textos.atrahasis.pasajes.3.fuente: Paraphrase based on Lambert and Millard (1969), Tablet III, i–viii
t.textos.atrahasis.pasajes.3.nota_academ: Tablet III is the direct source of Gilgamesh XI, which rewrites it in the first person. In the Old Babylonian poem there is no grant of immortality (the ending is damaged), but there is a structural solution to the problem that caused the flood: infant mortality, barrenness and the celibacy of certain priestesses (ugbabtu, entu, igiṣītu) are presented as divine institutions. The poem was also used as a ritual text in connection with childbirth.
t.textos.atrahasis.pasajes.3.lectura_act: Frymer-Kensky sees in the ending of Atrahasis a reflection on the limits of growth: the gods do not punish a moral sin but excess population, and the solution is birth control. She compares this approach with Genesis 9, where the covenant with Noah revolves instead around blood and violence.
Tikva Frymer-Kensky, "The Atrahasis Epic and Its Significance for Our Understanding of Genesis 1–9", Biblical Archaeologist 40, 1977
t.textos.diluvio-ziusudra.version: Old Babylonian version in Sumerian, preserved on a single, badly damaged tablet from Nippur (CBS 10673, c. 1600 BC), with a bilingual fragment from Nineveh
t.textos.diluvio-ziusudra.estructura.0.s: A god (probably Nintur or Enki) decides to save humanity from its scattering and have it build cities and temples. An, Enlil, Enki and Ninhursag create the "black-headed" people and the animals.
t.textos.diluvio-ziusudra.estructura.1.s: Kingship descends from heaven and the five antediluvian cities are founded (Eridu, Bad-tibira, Larak, Sippar, Shuruppak), each given to a god.
t.textos.diluvio-ziusudra.estructura.2.s: The gods decide on the flood; Inanna laments. The pious priest-king Ziusudra receives, beside a wall, the warning that the divine assembly has decided to destroy the seed of mankind.
t.textos.diluvio-ziusudra.estructura.3.s: Seven days and seven nights of flood toss the huge boat. Utu, the Sun, enters through an opening; Ziusudra sacrifices oxen and sheep. An and Enlil grant him a life like that of a god and settle him in Dilmun, where the sun rises.
t.textos.diluvio-ziusudra.pasajes.0.ref: Segments D–E (lines 201–260 of the continuous numbering)
t.textos.diluvio-ziusudra.pasajes.0.text: Paraphrase. All the winds and storms rise up at once and the flood sweeps over the cult centers. For seven days and seven nights the flood covers the land, and the waves and gales toss the huge boat. Then Utu, the Sun god, comes forth, illuminating heaven and earth. Ziusudra opens a window in the boat and the hero Utu enters with his rays. King Ziusudra prostrates himself before Utu and sacrifices oxen and countless sheep. Later, as the animals disembark, Ziusudra prostrates himself before An and Enlil, who treat him kindly: they grant him a life like that of a god and bestow on him eternal breath. Because he protected the seed of mankind and of the animals, they make him dwell in the land of Dilmun, "where the sun rises".
t.textos.diluvio-ziusudra.pasajes.0.fuen: Paraphrase based on ETCSL 1.7.4 (Black et al.) and on Civil (1969)
t.textos.diluvio-ziusudra.pasajes.0.nota: It is the oldest known version of the flood in narrative form, although the tablet preserves only a third of the text. Ziusudra means "life of long days". His name appears in some copies of the King List as king of Shuruppak, son of Ubara-Tutu, and in Greek (Berossus) as Xisuthros. The Sun entering through the window replaces the birds of the Akkadian versions. Arno Poebel published the tablet in 1914; the public-domain translations are unreliable today because of the advances in Sumerian.
t.textos.descenso-inanna.titulo: The Descent of Inanna to the Underworld
t.textos.descenso-inanna.version: Sumerian poem of about 410 lines, known from Old Babylonian copies (c. 1900–1600 BC), mainly from Nippur and Ur. There is also a much shorter Akkadian version, The Descent of Ishtar (about 140 lines), in Middle Assyrian and Neo-Assyrian copies from Assur and Nineveh
t.textos.descenso-inanna.estructura.0.si: Inanna "sets her mind" on the Underworld. She abandons her seven temples (Uruk, Bad-tibira, Zabalam, Adab, Nippur, Kish, Akkad) and dresses herself in seven attributes of power (me). She instructs her vizier Ninshubur: if she does not return in three days, Ninshubur must lament and ask Enlil, Nanna and Enki for help.
t.textos.descenso-inanna.estructura.1.si: At the gate of Ganzer, the gatekeeper Neti informs Ereshkigal, Inanna's sister, who orders the seven gates to be opened one by one. At each one Inanna is stripped of an attribute; to her protests she is told that the rites of the Underworld are perfect and must not be questioned. She arrives naked and bowed down.
t.textos.descenso-inanna.estructura.2.si: Inanna makes Ereshkigal rise and sits on her throne. The seven Anunna, judges of the Underworld, look at her with the look of death; she is turned into a corpse, hung on a hook.
t.textos.descenso-inanna.estructura.3.si: After three days, Ninshubur laments. Enlil and Nanna refuse to help, but Enki creates from the dirt under his fingernails two beings, the kurgarra and the gala-tura, with the food and water of life. They win Ereshkigal over by sympathizing with her pains and obtain the corpse. Inanna revives, but the Anunna demand a substitute.
t.textos.descenso-inanna.estructura.4.si: Inanna comes out escorted by galla demons. She spares Ninshubur and her sons Shara and Lulal, who mourn her dressed in sackcloth, but she finds her husband Dumuzi richly dressed and not in mourning, and hands him over. Dumuzi flees with Utu's help but is captured. In the end, Dumuzi and his sister Geshtinanna will take turns, half a year each, in the Underworld.
t.textos.descenso-inanna.pasajes.0.texto: "From the great heaven she set her mind on the great below". Paraphrase of the following lines: the same sentence is repeated with a change of subject ("the goddess", "Inanna"). My lady abandoned heaven, abandoned earth and went down to the Underworld. She abandoned her office of en and of lagar and went down. She abandoned the Eanna of Uruk, the Emush-kalama of Bad-tibira, the Giguna of Zabalam, the Esharra of Adab, the Barag-dur-ĝara of Nippur, the Hursaĝ-kalama of Kish and the Eulmash of Akkad.
t.textos.descenso-inanna.pasajes.0.fuent: Short quotation translated into Spanish from ETCSL 1.4.1 (Black et al., 1998–2006), lines 1–3, and here into English from the Spanish; the rest, paraphrase
t.textos.descenso-inanna.pasajes.0.nota_: The threefold repetition (the goddess, Inanna) is typical of Sumerian poetry. The "great below" (kur gal or ki-gal) is at once the mountain, foreign lands and the world of the dead. The list of temples she abandons maps the geography of her cult and amounts to renouncing her earthly power. No one in the text explains why she goes down: Inanna tells the gatekeepers that she has come to the funeral of Gugalanna, Ereshkigal's husband, but many scholars see an attempt to extend her dominion to the Underworld.
t.textos.descenso-inanna.pasajes.0.lectu: Sylvia Brinton Perera interprets the descent as the model of a process of female psychological initiation: stripping off social masks (the seven attributes), confronting the "dark sister" (Ereshkigal) and being reborn. The book was highly influential in feminist spirituality.
Sylvia Brinton Perera, Descent to the Goddess: A Way of Initiation for Women, 1981
